claims.text: A combined high-throughput DSC, high-temperature diffraction, and CALPHAD workflow can accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of HEAs.
The combined workflow will be more efficient than conventional characterization across the HEA family.
Preparing as-cast or homogenized alloys under inert or vacuum conditions ensures well-controlled composition and minimal contamination.
Rapid DSC scans can identify melting-related thermal events in these alloys.
In-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can track the volume change at melting.
CALPHAD can assess composition- and temperature-dependent thermodynamic behavior relevant to HEAs.
The measurements should extend from room temperature to slightly above each alloy's melting range under inert or vacuum atmosphere.
High-temperature diffraction provides real-time observation of lattice expansion and solid-to-liquid phase evolution.
CALPHAD databases provide computed Gibbs energies and phase equilibria over composition and temperature.
Calorimetric melting signals can supply melting onset or peak temperatures and fusion enthalpy.
Integrating calorimetry, diffraction, and thermodynamic predictions permits direct, self-consistent derivation of fusion properties and melting volume changes.
The integrated workflow captures the multicomponent interactions characteristic of HEAs.
Melting temperatures will be determined to within ±10–20 K.
Fusion enthalpy and entropy will be determined to within ±5%.
Melting volume changes will be determined to within ±1–2%.
Conventional single-sample DSC and simplified mixing rules have significantly larger uncertainties for compositionally complex HEAs.
The approach is most applicable to metallic multi-principal-element alloys with relatively simple crystal structures.
Accuracy will be lower for alloys with extensive chemical short-range order or complex stoichiometric intermetallic phases that current CALPHAD databases describe poorly.
Incomplete databases, instrumental calibration or scan-rate limits, and unmodeled metastable phases can produce inconsistencies.
Failure against independent control methods or reference materials within the stated uncertainty ranges would invalidate the approach.
